summary_paragraph: A man with a history of chronic alcohol use, CAD, CABG, COPD, and esophagitis was admitted for acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and tachypnea. He presented with leukocytosis, lactic acidosis, and an elevated anion gap, raising concern for sepsis or mesenteric ischemia. Imaging ruled out surgical causes but showed esophageal thickening and fatty liver. His symptoms were attributed to alcoholic gastritis and esophagitis. He developed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, managed initially with metoprolol and then transitioned to diltiazem due to symptomatic bradycardia. Electrolyte abnormalities, including hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatemia, were corrected. Pleural effusions developed, likely related to fluid shifts and atrial fibrillation, and were managed with diuresis. He improved with IV fluids, acid suppression, and alcohol cessation counseling. He was discharged on aspirin, diltiazem ER, and optimized GI medications, with strict instructions to abstain from alcohol and follow up with primary care, cardiology, and gastroenterology.
